'''Roger Kenneth Butlin''' is a British evolutionary biologist and professor at the [[University of Sheffield]]. He is known for his work on [[speciation]]. He served as [[Editor]] of ''[[Heredity (journal)|Heredity]]'' from 2009 to 2012, and President of the [[European Society for Evolutionary Biology]] from 2013 to 2015.<ref>https://eseb.org/society/officers/title=ESEB positions</ref> In 2015 he received the [[Darwin-Wallace Medal|Darwin Wallace Medal]] from the [[Linnean Society of London|Linnean Society]]<ref>https://www.linnean.org/news/2015/06/15/15th-june-2015-medal-winners</ref> and was appointed as a Distinguised Fellow of the [[European Society for Evolutionary Biology]] in 2019.<ref>https://eseb.org/prizes-funding/distinguished-fellows/</ref>. He is currently interim editor of the [[Biological Journal of the Linnean Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.linnean.org/news/2026/05/07/professor-roger-butlin-appointed-as-biological-journal-interim-editor-in-chief|title=Professor Roger Butlin appointed as Biological Journal Interim…|website=The Linnean Society|access-date=2026-10-18}}</ref>


==Education and career==
Butlin studied  Natural Sciences at [[Jesus College, Cambridge|Jesus College]] at the [[University of Cambridge]], graduating in 1976<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cienciavitae.pt/en/DF11-3390-07EC|title=Roger Kenneth Butlin (DF11-3390-07EC)|website=www.cienciavitae.pt|access-date=2026-10-18}}</ref>. He obtained his PhD in 1983 from the [[University of Nottingham]] working in the lab of Tom Day. Butlin then took a postdoctoral position in [[Godfrey Hewitt |Godfrey Hewitt's]] lab for two years at the [[University of East Anglia]]<ref>Ritchie MG, Butlin RK (2013). Godfrey M. Hewitt (1940-2013), President of ESEB 1999-2001. J Evol Biol 26: 691–692.</ref> In 1987 Butlin took a Royal Society Research Fellowship position at the [[University of Wales]] in Cardiff. In 1992 he became a lecturer at the [[University of Leeds]] and from 1994 as reader for evolutionary biology. He was  a professor at the [[University of Sheffield]] and [[University of Gothenburg]] until his retirement in 2025.<ref name="Faria2026">{{cite journal

==Work==
Butlin's work is concerned with understanding the genetics of speciation, focusing on reproductive isolation. As a model system, he examines insects and their acoustic and chemical signals, the inheritance of signal characteristics and female preferences. Besides insects, he also studies speciation and adaptation in periwinkles (''[[Littorina]]''). His work has contributed greatly to our current understanding of [[Ecological speciation]].

==Selected publications==

* "What do we need to know about speciation?", ''Trends Ecol Evol''<ref>Butlin R, Debelle A, Kerth C, Snook RR (2012). What do we need to know about speciation? Trends Ecol Evol. 27: 27-39</ref>
* "Reinforcement: an idea evolving", ''Trends Ecol Evol''<ref>Butlin RK (1995). Reinforcement: an idea evolving. Trends Ecol Evol 10: 432–434.</ref>
* "The costs and benefits of sex: new insights from old asexual lineages." ''[[Nature Reviews Genetics]]''<ref>Butlin R (2002). The costs and benefits of sex: new insights from old asexual lineages. Nat Rev Genet 3: 311.</ref>
* "Variation in female mate preference across a grasshopper hybrid zone."''[[Journal of Evolutionary Biology]]''<ref>Butlin RK, Ritchie MG (1991). Variation in female mate preference across a grasshopper hybrid zone. J Evol Biol 4: 227–240.</ref>
* "Coupling, Reinforcement, and Speciation".''[[The American Naturalist]]''<ref>Butlin RK, Smadja CM (2018). Coupling, Reinforcement, and Speciation. Am Nat 191: 155–172.</ref>
* "Male spermatophore investment increases female fecundity in a grasshopper. ''[[Evolution (journal)|Evolution]]''<ref>Butlin RK, Woodhatch CW, Hewitt GM (1987). Male spermatophore investment increases female fecundity in a grasshopper. Evolution 41: 221–225.</ref>
* "A framework for comparing processes of speciation in the presence of gene flow." ''[[Molecular Ecology]]''<ref>Smadja CM, Butlin RK (2011). A framework for comparing processes of speciation in the presence of gene flow. Mol Ecol 20: 5123–5140.</ref>
